screens.title: Using Paramiko and Netmiko for SSH Automation
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson you'll learn why SSH-based automation still matters even when modern APIs exist, and how two Python libraries—Paramiko and Netmiko—fit into everyday network engineering. Many production routers and switches still expose only a command-line interface over SSH. That means you will sometimes have to run automated commands and collect output by logging in just like an operator would. Paramiko offers a powerful, low-level SSHv2 implementation that gives you fine-grained control over sessions, but it forces you to manage byte streams, terminal prompts, and interactive shells. Netmiko builds on that foundation and abstracts device differences, pagination, and configuration mode so you can focus on commands and logic. Over the screens that follow, we'll inspect a Paramiko example to see where complexity arises, then switch to Netmiko examples that show how to connect, run show commands, push config, save changes, and handle errors. We will also cover secure credential handling, common mistakes such as wrong device type or hardcoded passwords, and a hands-on script to configure a loopback and an interface on Cisco IOS XE. By the end, you will understand trade-offs and have a practical script template you can adapt safely in a lab environment. What real device would you automate first after this lesson?

Learn when to use low-level SSH control and when to prefer a device-aware abstraction for reliable CLI automation.

Many legacy devices only offer CLI over SSH. You will still need SSH automation for them.
Approach
Use Paramiko for low-level control and Netmiko for robust, multi-vendor CLI tasks.

Device-aware abstraction that handles prompts, pagination, and config mode for many vendors.

screens.title: Why SSH automation is still essential
screens.narratorSegment: Begin with a clear definition: SSH-based automation is programmatic interaction with a device's command-line interface over Secure Shell. This is necessary when devices do not support structured APIs like NETCONF or RESTCONF, which offer predictable, schema-driven data. In many enterprise networks, older router and switch models still expose only a CLI. The consequence is that scripts must log in and interact with the same textual interface a human operator uses. That leads to screen scraping—parsing text designed for humans, not machines. Screen scraping is fragile because the exact output can change across OS versions, prompt formats, or localized messages. A practical example is running a single show command across 50 routers and relying on string splits to extract the neighbor state; a minor prompt change can break your parser. A common misconception is that SSH automation is inherently bad; it is not. It is indispensable for unsupported devices, but it demands defensive coding practices: retries, strict prompt detection, and verification steps. Takeaway: treat CLI automation as a migration path—use it when necessary, but keep an eye on replacing brittle parsing with structured output when devices allow it. Which devices in your estate must remain CLI-driven?

screens.title: Paramiko: low-level SSH control
screens.narratorSegment: Paramiko is a pure-Python implementation of SSHv2 that gives you the building blocks for client and server functionality. It exposes methods to open SSH connections, execute commands, and transfer files via SFTP. When you use Paramiko directly you manage stdin, stdout, and stderr streams and decode byte data into strings. For non-interactive commands exec_command is often enough, but for multi-step configuration you must invoke a pseudo-terminal with invoke_shell and implement your own prompt detection and pagination handling. Here's a concrete example: using exec_command to run a show command returns byte streams which you then decode. The real-world challenge appears when you need to enter configuration mode; you then have to emulate a human operator, send commands, and read until you detect the prompt. A common misconception is that Paramiko always gives better results; in fact, while it's more flexible it also exposes you to fragile parsing and higher maintenance. If you need deep protocol control or custom SFTP flows, Paramiko is ideal; otherwise, consider higher-level libraries that handle device quirks for you. How would you detect prompt changes in a mixed IOS fleet?

keyIdea.text: Powerful low-level control but requires manual session, prompt, and pagination handling that can be fragile for CLIs.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.4 › Paramiko
What Paramiko gives you
  • SSHv2 client and server capabilities, including SFTP for file transfers.
  • Direct access to exec_command and invoke_shell for interactive sessions.
  • Full control over authentication and host key policies.
Concrete snippet
import paramiko

hostname = '192.168.1.10'
port = 22
username = 'admin'
password = 'your_password'

try:
    client = paramiko.SSHClient()
    client.set_missing_host_key_policy(paramiko.AutoAddPolicy())  # insecure for prod
    client.connect(hostname=hostname, port=port, username=username, password=password, look_for_keys=False)

    stdin, stdout, stderr = client.exec_command('show ip interface brief')
    output = stdout.read().decode()
    error = stderr.read().decode()

    if output:
        print('Command Output:')
        print(output)
    if error:
        print('Error Output:')
        print(error)

finally:
    client.close()
Why this can be complex
Interactive sessions
invoke_shell requires manual prompt detection, reading until expected prompt strings, and handling pagination like --More--.
Pitfall
Parsing raw output is brittle; slight CLI differences break parsers if not written defensively.
Key Takeaway

Use Paramiko for low-level needs but prefer device-aware libraries for routine automation to reduce maintenance.

screens.title: Managing interactive sessions with Paramiko
screens.narratorSegment: When you need interactive control—such as entering configuration mode or responding to device prompts—Paramiko's invoke_shell allows you to open a pseudo-terminal and emulate an operator. A reliable process helps avoid race conditions and truncated output. Start by opening the shell and setting a reasonable timeout. Then send a command and read until you detect the device prompt; avoid blind sleeps because they make scripts slow and brittle. Handle pagination by detecting common markers like --More-- and sending space or specific sequences to continue. When entering and exiting configuration mode, explicitly verify the prompt change that indicates you are in config mode so subsequent commands run in the intended context. Include try-except blocks to catch SSH exceptions and ensure the channel is closed in a finally clause. A common misconception is that adding sleep calls fixes timing issues; it only masks race conditions and creates slow, unreliable automation. Instead, prefer prompt-aware reads, timeouts, and small retries. Example scenario: you open invoke_shell to enter config mode, set an interface description, verify the running-config, and then save. Always verify changes in the device output and log both success and errors for post-run audits. How will you confirm the prompt reliably across device variants?

Module 8 › Chapter 8.4 › Interactive Sessions
Process: Use invoke_shell safely
Step 1
Open shell and set timeout
Create a channel with a reasonable timeout to avoid indefinite blocking and resource leaks.
Step 2
Send and read until prompt
Implement reads that stop when the expected prompt is seen instead of using fixed sleeps.
Step 3
Handle pagination
Detect --More-- prompts and send the correct continuation key programmatically.
Step 4
Verify mode changes
Confirm prompt changes when entering config mode before sending configuration commands.
Step 5
Exception and cleanup
Wrap session handling in try-except-finally to ensure channels and clients close cleanly.
Scenario
Open shell, enter config, change interface description, verify running-config, then save and close with logs for audit.
Key Takeaway

Prompt-aware reading and explicit verification are the core techniques that prevent fragile, timing-based scripts.

screens.title: Netmiko vs Paramiko
screens.narratorSegment: Let's contrast the two libraries so you can choose the right tool. Paramiko is low-level: it implements SSHv2 and gives you direct control over channels, exec calls, and SFTP. That control is useful when you need custom SSH features or advanced file transfers. Netmiko, by contrast, sits on top of Paramiko and other SSH backends and provides a device-aware A P I tailored to network equipment. Netmiko detects prompts, handles pagination, and provides helper methods like send_command and send_config_set that automatically enter and exit configuration mode. A concrete example highlights the difference: running a show command with Paramiko requires managing stdout and decoding; running the same with Netmiko is a single send_command call that returns text. Common misconceptions include thinking Netmiko hides all parsing work—Netmiko simplifies the session but you remain responsible for interpreting the returned CLI text unless you plug in parsers. In practice, use Netmiko for routine, multi-vendor tasks and reserve Paramiko when you need low-level SSH features. The right choice minimizes maintenance and keeps scripts readable and reliable. Netmiko vs Paramiko means use netmiko for device-focused cli automation and paramiko for low-level ssh needs or custom protocols.. In practical terms, when to choose a high-level abstraction over low-level control. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 8 › Chapter 8.4 › Netmiko vs Paramiko
Paramiko (low-level)
  • Exec and shell channels with direct bytes streams.
  • SFTP file transfers and custom authentication control.
  • Greater flexibility but more session handling code.
Netmiko (high-level)
  • Device-specific helpers: ConnectHandler, send_command, send_config_set.
  • Automatic prompt detection and pagination handling.
  • Faster to write and easier to maintain for device automation.
Concrete contrast
With Paramiko you manage stdin/stdout and decode bytes. With Netmiko you call send_command and get back text, with the library handling prompts and timeouts. Netmiko shortens scripts and reduces prompt-handling bugs for common network tasks.
Key Takeaway

Pick Netmiko for routine device automation; use Paramiko when you need custom SSH features that Netmiko doesn't expose.

The device dictionary specifies device_type, host, username, password, port, and optionally secret for enable mode. When you wrap ConnectHandler in a with statement, Netmiko ensures the connection closes cleanly. Use send_command for single operational commands; Netmiko waits for the expected prompt and handles pagination. A concrete example from the chapter shows how to run show ip interface brief and loop through multiple commands, printing each result. Common mistakes include selecting the wrong device_type; that can break prompt detection. Another is forgetting to pass secret when your session requires enable for privileged commands. Netmiko does not automatically parse output into structured data—you receive CLI text. If you need structured output, pair Netmiko with TextFSM templates or Genie parsers. For reliability, test commands in a lab and confirm expected prompt behavior. After testing, ask: which show commands in your environment require enable mode? Module 8 › Chapter 8.4 › Netmiko Quickstart
Minimal device dict
device = {'{'} 'device_type': 'cisco_ios', 'host': '192.168.1.10', 'username': 'admin', 'password': 'your_password', 'port': 22, 'secret': 'enable_password' {'}'}
Concrete snippet
from netmiko import ConnectHandler

device = {
    "device_type": "cisco_ios",
    "host": "192.168.1.10",
    "username": "admin",
    "password": "your_password",
    "port": 22,
    "secret": "enable_password"
}

with ConnectHandler(**device) as net_connect:
    output = net_connect.send_command("show ip interface brief")
    print(output)
Notes and best practices
  • Wrap ConnectHandler with with to auto-close connections even on errors.
  • Test device_type values; wrong type breaks prompt detection.
  • Use secret if enable is required for privileged commands.
Key Takeaway

Netmiko reduces session boilerplate and prompt handling so you can focus on commands and verification logic.

screens.title: Sending configuration with send_config_set
screens.narratorSegment: Netmiko simplifies configuration changes through send_config_set, which takes a list of configuration commands and handles entering and exiting configuration mode automatically. This reduces a common source of bugs: forgetting to exit config mode or sending commands in the wrong context. Use send_config_set for atomic groups of related commands, such as creating an interface and setting its description. Always include verification steps: after send_config_set, run show running-config on the updated interface to confirm the change. Also save the running configuration with save_config to persist changes. A concrete example configures Loopback0, sets an IP address, and configures a physical interface description and no shutdown. Wrap the config sequence in a try-except block so network errors or authentication failures don't leave the device in a partially configured state. A common mistake is assuming send_config_set is idempotent; it is not inherently idempotent—you should write commands or checks that avoid applying repeated changes when unnecessary. After applying changes in a lab, run verification commands to confirm results before moving to production. Sending configuration with send_config_set means send_config_set handles mode transitions for you; always verify and save changes, and code defensively for partial failures.. screens.title: Secure credential management
screens.narratorSegment: Managing credentials securely is essential for any automation system. Never hardcode usernames or passwords in scripts. Instead, prefer environment variables, configuration files with strict permissions, or a proper secrets management solution. The chapter provides an example using os. getenv to load NETMIKO_HOST, NETMIKO_USERNAME, NETMIKO_PASSWORD, and NETMIKO_SECRET. This allows you to keep secrets out of source control and rotate credentials without editing code. For teams, integrate your automation with a secrets manager so scripts fetch ephemeral credentials or tokens at runtime. A common mistake is fallback values in code that contain real credentials; even placeholders can be accidentally committed or misused. Another misconception is that environment variables are always secure; they reduce risk but should be combined with process isolation and access controls. After credentials are loaded, limit logging of sensitive fields—log host and operation results, but redact passwords in logs. Finally, test credential handling in a lab to ensure your automation fails safely when secrets are missing or invalid. screens.title: Parsing CLI output: raw text vs structured data
screens.narratorSegment: Netmiko returns raw CLI text for commands, which leaves parsing and structuring the result to you. Simple scripts may extract fields with splits or regular expressions, but this approach is brittle because CLI formatting can change. Two well-known parsing aids are TextFSM and Genie. TextFSM uses templates that match command output patterns and convert them into record rows and columns. Genie provides richer, vendor-specific parsing and integrates with pyATS for advanced validation. A practical example: extracting interface status—text parsing can work for a consistent fleet, but TextFSM templates make the result resilient to spacing changes. A common misconception is that parsing libraries remove the need to understand output: they still require correct templates and validation. When planning automation, prefer structured parsers for production runs, and keep a fallback strategy that logs raw output for debugging. For one-off ad-hoc checks, simple text parsing may suffice, but for repeated, fleet-wide automation, invest in templates and structured transforms. fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson you'll learn why SSH-based automation still matters even when modern APIs exist, and how two Python libraries—Paramiko and Netmiko—fit into everyday network engineering. Many production routers and switches still expose only a command-line interface over SSH. That means you will sometimes have to run automated commands and collect output by logging in just like an operator would. Paramiko offers a powerful, low-level SSHv2 implementation that gives you fine-grained control over sessions, but it forces you to manage byte streams, terminal prompts, and interactive shells. Netmiko builds on that foundation and abstracts device differences, pagination, and configuration mode so you can focus on commands and logic. Over the screens that follow, we'll inspect a Paramiko example to see where complexity arises, then switch to Netmiko examples that show how to connect, run show commands, push config, save changes, and handle errors. We will also cover secure credential handling, common mistakes such as wrong device type or hardcoded passwords, and a hands-on script to configure a loopback and an interface on Cisco IOS XE. By the end, you will understand trade-offs and have a practical script template you can adapt safely in a lab environment. What real device would you automate first after this lesson?

These objectives lay out the practical skills you'll gain. First, you will understand the limitations of screen scraping and why structured APIs are preferred when available. That means recognizing where CLI parsing fails and when SSH is the only option. Second, you'll be able to explain Paramiko's role as a low-level SSHv2 library: what it offers, when to use invoke_shell, and why raw byte streams demand careful decoding and prompt detection. Third, you'll practice using Netmiko for day-to-day network tasks: creating a ConnectHandler, sending show commands, handling pagination, entering config mode, and saving changes. Finally, you'll develop Python scripts to retrieve configuration and make changes on Cisco IOS XE devices while applying secure credential handling. Each objective emphasizes not only the how but the why—this helps you choose safer, more maintainable automation strategies in production-like labs. As you study the examples, think about which objective you want to master first and how you will validate it in a lab environment.

These additional objectives focus on the practical tasks you'll perform. You'll learn to develop Python scripts that execute commands and retrieve configuration from Cisco IOS XE devices using Netmiko, including the ConnectHandler pattern and saving changes. You will implement robust error handling: learn to catch connection timeouts, authentication failures, and unexpected device prompts so scripts can log, retry, or fail gracefully. Secure credential management is emphasized: environment variables, configuration files with restricted permissions, or a secrets manager are preferred over embedded passwords. Finally, you will practice parsing output: while Netmiko returns raw CLI text, you'll learn when to pair it with parsers like TextFSM or Genie to transform CLI into structured data. Together these skills help you automate repetitive tasks reliably, reduce risk during changes, and scale operations across many devices when APIs are not available.

Begin with a clear definition: SSH-based automation is programmatic interaction with a device's command-line interface over Secure Shell. This is necessary when devices do not support structured APIs like NETCONF or RESTCONF, which offer predictable, schema-driven data. In many enterprise networks, older router and switch models still expose only a CLI. The consequence is that scripts must log in and interact with the same textual interface a human operator uses. That leads to screen scraping—parsing text designed for humans, not machines. Screen scraping is fragile because the exact output can change across OS versions, prompt formats, or localized messages. A practical example is running a single show command across 50 routers and relying on string splits to extract the neighbor state; a minor prompt change can break your parser. A common misconception is that SSH automation is inherently bad; it is not. It is indispensable for unsupported devices, but it demands defensive coding practices: retries, strict prompt detection, and verification steps. Takeaway: treat CLI automation as a migration path—use it when necessary, but keep an eye on replacing brittle parsing with structured output when devices allow it. Which devices in your estate must remain CLI-driven?

Paramiko is a pure-Python implementation of SSHv2 that gives you the building blocks for client and server functionality. It exposes methods to open SSH connections, execute commands, and transfer files via SFTP. When you use Paramiko directly you manage stdin, stdout, and stderr streams and decode byte data into strings. For non-interactive commands exec_command is often enough, but for multi-step configuration you must invoke a pseudo-terminal with invoke_shell and implement your own prompt detection and pagination handling. Here's a concrete example: using exec_command to run a show command returns byte streams which you then decode. The real-world challenge appears when you need to enter configuration mode; you then have to emulate a human operator, send commands, and read until you detect the prompt. A common misconception is that Paramiko always gives better results; in fact, while it's more flexible it also exposes you to fragile parsing and higher maintenance. If you need deep protocol control or custom SFTP flows, Paramiko is ideal; otherwise, consider higher-level libraries that handle device quirks for you. How would you detect prompt changes in a mixed IOS fleet?

When you need interactive control—such as entering configuration mode or responding to device prompts—Paramiko's invoke_shell allows you to open a pseudo-terminal and emulate an operator. A reliable process helps avoid race conditions and truncated output. Start by opening the shell and setting a reasonable timeout. Then send a command and read until you detect the device prompt; avoid blind sleeps because they make scripts slow and brittle. Handle pagination by detecting common markers like --More-- and sending space or specific sequences to continue. When entering and exiting configuration mode, explicitly verify the prompt change that indicates you are in config mode so subsequent commands run in the intended context. Include try-except blocks to catch SSH exceptions and ensure the channel is closed in a finally clause. A common misconception is that adding sleep calls fixes timing issues; it only masks race conditions and creates slow, unreliable automation. Instead, prefer prompt-aware reads, timeouts, and small retries. Example scenario: you open invoke_shell to enter config mode, set an interface description, verify the running-config, and then save. Always verify changes in the device output and log both success and errors for post-run audits. How will you confirm the prompt reliably across device variants?

Let's contrast the two libraries so you can choose the right tool. Paramiko is low-level: it implements SSHv2 and gives you direct control over channels, exec calls, and SFTP. That control is useful when you need custom SSH features or advanced file transfers. Netmiko, by contrast, sits on top of Paramiko and other SSH backends and provides a device-aware A P I tailored to network equipment. Netmiko detects prompts, handles pagination, and provides helper methods like send_command and send_config_set that automatically enter and exit configuration mode. A concrete example highlights the difference: running a show command with Paramiko requires managing stdout and decoding; running the same with Netmiko is a single send_command call that returns text. Common misconceptions include thinking Netmiko hides all parsing work—Netmiko simplifies the session but you remain responsible for interpreting the returned CLI text unless you plug in parsers. In practice, use Netmiko for routine, multi-vendor tasks and reserve Paramiko when you need low-level SSH features. The right choice minimizes maintenance and keeps scripts readable and reliable. Netmiko vs Paramiko means use netmiko for device-focused cli automation and paramiko for low-level ssh needs or custom protocols.. In practical terms, when to choose a high-level abstraction over low-level control. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Netmiko is designed to make connecting and running commands on network devices straightforward. The core pattern is a device dictionary and ConnectHandler.
